html.ReLoopVSR restores a video stream withou: ReLoopVSR restores a video stream without future frames, in one denoising step per frame. It aligns and re-noises the previous restoration, refines it with the current low-resolution frame, and restarts wherever errors are predicted or the scene cuts. It leads in perceptual quality with far lower memory and latency, and ReLoopVSR-fast exceeds 240 FPS at 720p.

html.<b>Streaming video super-resolution with: Streaming video super-resolution with ReLoopVSR (paper Fig. 1). ReLoopVSR propagates the previous restoration and refines it with the current observation in a single denoising step. It combines competitive fidelity, temporal consistency and throughput with zero future-frame dependency, the shortest measured time to first frame, and the lowest peak memory usage among the evaluated methods.

html.Streaming VSR reconstructs high-resoluti: Streaming VSR reconstructs high-resolution frames as low-resolution observations arrive, without future frames and within a bounded per-frame budget. After motion compensation, previously restored content already estimates the current frame, so ReLoopVSR corrects that estimate instead of generating each frame from noise. At frame k, the output depends only on the current low-resolution input and a fixed-size recurrent state that caches latents, RGB outputs and decoder features.
html.The previous denoised latent is aligned: The previous denoised latent is aligned to the current frame, re-noised so that inherited detail can be revised, and refined in one denoising step conditioned on the current observation. Repeated updates to temporally corresponding content form a spatiotemporal momentum, which extends effective computational depth with fixed parameters.
html.However, alignment errors, disocclusions: However, alignment errors, disocclusions, lighting changes and scene cuts invalidate inherited content and cause error spiking. Local and global reliability control therefore truncates this momentum on the fly, restarting unreliable tiles from the current LR observation and resetting the full state at global changes.
html.Because each output becomes the starting: Because each output becomes the starting point of the next frame, the model is trained on its own streaming rollouts and then with perceptual temporal supervision, so that it learns to correct inherited errors.
html.Animated schematic comparing how three k: Animated schematic comparing how three kinds of method produce frame k
html.Pipeline over consecutive frames. Each r: Pipeline over consecutive frames. Each row warps the previous denoised latent to frame k by optical flow, lets reliability control keep reliable tiles or restart the others from the encoded LR frame, re-noises the result and refines it with one shared denoising step, and decodes it with cached decoder features. The adapter carries guidance from the previous output. At a scene cut the state is reset.
html.<b>Recurrent autoregressive refinement i: Recurrent autoregressive refinement in ReLoopVSR (paper Fig. 3). A shared one-step denoiser restores each frame from the previous restoration: the denoised latent is warped to frame k, re-noised, and refined with the current LR frame, while the adapter and cached decoder features carry guidance from the previous output. Reliability control (DEN) keeps reliable tiles, restarts unreliable tiles from the encoded LR frame, and resets the full state at scene cuts.
html.ReLoopVSR uses the previous restoration: ReLoopVSR uses the previous restoration as an initial estimate. Optical flow between the bicubic ×4-upsampled current and previous LR inputs aligns the cached denoised latent to frame k. The aligned latent is re-noised to an intermediate level and refined in a single denoising step, and the refined latent is cached as the state for the next frame.
html.As in SDEdit and ResShift, re-noising le: As in SDEdit and ResShift, re-noising lets the current observation revise inherited detail. Stream-DiffVSR, by contrast, starts each four-step trajectory from noise and uses the previous restoration only as a condition.
html.The design is inspired by looped Transfo: The design is inspired by looped Transformers, which reuse shared parameters across iterations to increase effective depth in a compact model. Here the iterations run across frames, at one denoising step per frame.
html.On YouHQ40 and REDS4, starting from enco: On YouHQ40 and REDS4, starting from encoded LR instead of the propagated latent leaves spatial scores nearly unchanged but raises tLP by 12%, and removing the whole recurrent state raises tLP most, from 0.596 to 1.093.
html.Top: a film strip with two scene cuts, w: Top: a film strip with two scene cuts, where ReLoopVSR uses the current and past frames since the last cut while a chunk-based DiT buffers n future frames across a cut. Bottom: ReLoopVSR warps the previous output with LR flow, re-noises the aligned result, refines it in one distilled step with the current LR frame, and feeds the new output back as recurrent refinement.
html.<b>Streaming input and recurrent refinem: Streaming input and recurrent refinement (paper Fig. 2). Chunk-based DiT methods buffer n future frames, adding latency and mixing in unrelated content across cuts; ReLoopVSR uses only current and past frames since the last cut, autoregressively building spatiotemporal momentum through recurrent refinement.

html.In consistent scenes the propagated rest: In consistent scenes the propagated restoration strengthens a compact model, but local inconsistencies such as moving people and global ones such as lighting changes and scene cuts cause error spiking when they are propagated. A lightweight Dynamic Estimation Network (DEN) therefore predicts the restoration error of the aligned latent from the current LR input, the warped previous LR input and the aligned latent.
html.Locally, tiles with low predicted error: Locally, tiles with low predicted error keep the aligned restoration, and the remaining tiles restart from the encoded bicubic-upsampled observation. Both sources share one denoising step, so restarts add no denoiser evaluation.
html.Globally, the full state resets when unr: Globally, the full state resets when unreliable tiles cover at least half of the frame and a global LR appearance change is detected. The reset also clears the temporal conditions and the flow warm start, and it needs no future frames.
html.Disabling reliability control raises LPI: Disabling reliability control raises LPIPS at 29 cut events from 0.0820 to 0.1088, so the benefit comes from full resets.
html.Illustration of reliability control: loc: Illustration of reliability control: locally, reliable tiles keep the aligned restoration while unreliable tiles restart from the current LR observation; globally, a scene cut resets the state and clears the temporal conditions.
html.<b>Local and global reliability control<: Local and global reliability control (paper Fig. 4). Locally, reliable tiles keep the aligned restoration, while unreliable tiles stop the momentum and restart from the current LR observation. Globally, scene-cut resets also clear temporal conditions.
html.The backbone is trained for this formula: The backbone is trained for this formulation within a fixed per-frame budget, in four stages: spatial adaptation, one-step distillation, self-rollout fine-tuning and temporal fine-tuning.
html.Spatial adaptation teaches the U-Net to: Spatial adaptation teaches the U-Net to refine re-noised propagated estimates with spatially varying corruption, and one-step distillation compresses within-frame refinement from a shared initial latent.
html.Self-rollout fine-tuning replays detache: Self-rollout fine-tuning replays detached, model-generated streaming states, including restarts, resets and cached decoder features, against the frozen initial student, and alternately updates the denoiser, adapter and temporal decoder. A flow-masked consistency loss matches temporal residuals to the ground truth, and a no-reference quality term adds MUSIQ and CLIP-IQA.
html.Temporal fine-tuning then adds a loss th: Temporal fine-tuning then adds a loss that matches the magnitude of inter-frame perceptual change to the ground truth within shots. On REDS4 it lowers tLP from 0.682 to 0.301.
html.Training recipe in three panels: spatial: Training recipe in three panels: spatial adaptation against a four-step teacher, one-step distillation against a two-step teacher from the same start, and self-rollout fine-tuning with alternating updates of the denoiser, adapter and temporal decoder on detached self-rollout records, with the frozen initial student as reference, the rollout loss, and a consistency loss along ground-truth flow.
html.<b>Training recipe of ReLoopVSR</b> (pap: Training recipe of ReLoopVSR (paper Fig. 5). (a) Spatial adaptation trains the U-Net to refine re-noised propagated estimates. (b) One-step distillation compresses within-frame refinement using a shared initial latent. (c) Self-rollout fine-tuning alternately updates the denoiser, adapter and temporal decoder on detached model-generated states, with the frozen initial student as a reference.
html.Since the initial latent already carries: Since the initial latent already carries restored content, temporal guidance can focus on refining it. A ControlNet-style encoder that re-extracts features from the previous RGB output costs a great deal relative to one-step denoising, so ReLoopVSR uses a compact adapter and cached decoder features instead.
html.The convolutional temporal adapter (25.7: The convolutional temporal adapter (25.7M parameters) takes the denoiser input, the warped previous output and the DEN map, and produces 13 residuals. A gate predicted from the DEN map attenuates guidance in unreliable regions, and the adapter is bypassed on the first frame and at cuts.
html.The temporal decoder aligns and fuses ca: The temporal decoder aligns and fuses cached block features through zero-initialized residuals, which avoids re-extraction from the previous RGB output and limits high-resolution cost.
html.Block diagrams of the temporal adapter,: Block diagrams of the temporal adapter, the temporal decoder with warped cached features, the fast decoder for non-keyframes, the DEN error predictor, and tile selection with scene-cut reset.
html.<b>Temporal modules and reliability cont: Temporal modules and reliability control (supplement). (a) Adapter conditioned on reliability and noise level. (b) Decoder fusing warped cached features. (c) Fast decoder for non-keyframes. (d) DEN predicting the error of the aligned latent. (e) Tile selection and scene-cut reset.
html.Adjacent frames are temporally redundant: Adjacent frames are temporally redundant, so most frames can be updated from the recurrent state without a new diffusion step. In the spirit of SlowFast networks, ReLoopVSR-fast applies one-step diffusion only to keyframes and restores the frames in between with a lightweight fast decoder that uses the current LR input and gated, aligned history. It remains causal and emits each frame at once.
html.Keyframes begin with the first frame and: Keyframes begin with the first frame and recur at a nominal interval K; LR appearance changes trigger earlier keyframes, and every keyframe uses reliability control. K=0 denotes ReLoopVSR-base.
html.A larger <i>K</i> amortizes the denoiser: A larger K amortizes the denoiser over more frames at some cost in fidelity. Training follows the base recipe, plus backpropagation through time (BPTT) for the fast decoder.
html.Five consecutive frames k to k+4. Frames: Five consecutive frames k to k+4. Frames k and k+4 pass through one-step diffusion and refresh the keyframe cache of latent, RGB and features; frames k+1 to k+3 use a fast decoder that receives the current LR frame, keyframe references aligned by composed flow, and the previous RGB output. Red arrows mark BPTT gradients across the fast-decoder frames.
html.<b>Fast streaming inference</b> (<i>K</i: Fast streaming inference (K=4 example; paper Fig. 6). Diffusion updates refresh keyframe caches, and a lightweight fast decoder restores the intervening frames. Blue paths align cached references by composed flow, gray paths carry the previous RGB output, and red arrows show the BPTT gradients used to fine-tune the fast decoder. LR appearance changes can trigger earlier keyframes.

html.ReLoopVSR is a compact recurrent autoreg: ReLoopVSR is a compact recurrent autoregressive diffusion framework for streaming ×4 video super-resolution. It aligns and re-noises the previous denoised latent to initialize the current update and refines it with the current low-resolution observation through a shared one-step denoiser. Lightweight temporal modules reduce conditioning and decoding costs.
html.Local and global reliability control sto: Local and global reliability control stops the propagation where errors are predicted, and rollout training with perceptual temporal supervision adapts the model to correct inherited errors. ReLoopVSR-fast runs the denoiser only on keyframes and restores the other frames with a lightweight fast decoder.
html.Within a scene, the previous restoration: Within a scene, the previous restoration, after motion compensation, already estimates the current frame, so correcting it is cheaper than generating the frame again from noise. Each update depends only on inputs that have already arrived, so no future-frame buffering is needed.
html.Repeated updates with the same denoiser: Repeated updates with the same denoiser on temporally corresponding content extend the effective computational depth across frames, with fixed parameters and one denoising step per frame.
html.ReLoopVSR-base runs one denoising step o: ReLoopVSR-base runs one denoising step on every frame and offers the best fidelity. ReLoopVSR-fast runs the denoiser only on keyframes, at a nominal interval K from 4 to 20, and restores the frames in between with a 3.70M-parameter fast decoder. On REDS4, K=4 gives 85.7 FPS and K=20 gives 249.4 FPS at 720p in half precision, at some cost in fidelity.
html.The full state resets when unreliable ti: The full state resets when unreliable tiles cover at least half of the frame and a global LR appearance change is detected through a large color-histogram distance or low thumbnail correlation with the previous frame. The latent, the temporal conditions and the flow warm start are cleared together, using no future frames.
html.All 121 cuts in the full-film <i>Tears o: All 121 cuts in the full-film Tears of Steel streams are detected, and 29 of 34 cut pairs on LongAIGC-4. Strong lighting flashes can also trigger resets.
html.How does it compare with other methods?: How does it compare with other methods?
html.ReLoopVSR achieves the lowest LPIPS and: ReLoopVSR achieves the lowest LPIPS and DISTS on all six paired benchmarks, the lowest tOF on all six and the lowest tLP on five. Under the common 720p protocol it depends on no future frames and has the shortest time to first frame and the lowest peak memory among the measured methods.
However, it does not lead every metric. Larger diffusion priors lead MUSIQ on every paired set, DOVE leads SSIM and VMAF on Vid4 and SPMCS, and bicubic upsampling itself tops SSIM on LongAIGC-8.
html.ReLoopVSR-fast exceeds 240 FPS at 720p a: ReLoopVSR-fast exceeds 240 FPS at 720p and 28 FPS at 4K in half precision on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. ReLoopVSR-base runs at 17.4 FPS at 720p in FP16 and at 3.58 FPS in strict FP32. Both are streaming in the causal sense, because each output is available without waiting for future frames.
html.How much GPU memory does it need? Does i: How much GPU memory does it need? Does it run out of memory on long videos?
html.At 720p, peak allocation is 4.92 GiB for: At 720p, peak allocation is 4.92 GiB for ReLoopVSR in strict FP32, 4.4 GiB for ReLoopVSR-base in FP16, and 2.2 GiB for ReLoopVSR-fast. In half precision, ReLoopVSR restores 4K video with 11.6 GiB of peak memory. The state has a fixed size and frames are processed one at a time, so memory stays constant with stream length.
html.The evaluated model restores ×4 only, an: The evaluated model restores ×4 only, and other scale factors remain unevaluated.
html.Why might results look close to bicubic: Why might results look close to bicubic on my own video?
html.The default model is trained for bicubic: The default model is trained for bicubic ×4 inputs. Compressed or otherwise degraded video needs the real-world fine-tuned checkpoint, which is the version used for VideoLQ in the table above. Even then, gains depend on content and metric. Check also that the input is the low-resolution source rather than an already upscaled video.

js.sch.each_new_frame_starts_from_noise_and: Each new frame starts from noise and takes four denoising steps, with the previous restoration used as conditioning. Detail is therefore generated again at every frame.
js.sch.regenerate_each_frame_noise_enters_a: Regenerate each frame. Noise enters a chain of four denoising steps conditioned on the previous restoration and the current low-resolution frame, which produces the restored frame k.
js.sch.the_method_buffers_a_chunk_that_incl: The method buffers a chunk that includes future frames and restores the chunk jointly. The output for frame k therefore waits for frames that have not yet arrived.
js.sch.re_restore_chunks_frames_including_f: Re-restore chunks. Frames including future frames accumulate in a buffered chunk, which is restored jointly, and frame k is then taken from the restored chunk.
js.sch.reloopvsr_warps_the_previous_restore: ReLoopVSR warps the previous restored latent to frame k and restarts unreliable tiles from the encoded LR. One U-Net step then refines the re-noised start, and the output becomes the starting point of the next frame.
js.sch.reloopvsr_the_previous_restored_late: ReLoopVSR. The previous restored latent is warped to frame k by optical flow between the upsampled low-resolution inputs. A reliability check selects per tile between the aligned latent and the encoded low-resolution frame, and a scene cut resets the state to the encoded low-resolution frame. The selected start is re-noised to an intermediate level and refined by one U-Net step under the current low-resolution frame. The restored frame k loops back as the starting point of frame k+1.
